## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{0}{0}{100}{0}{0}{0}
\end{marginfigure}

_Why must the decision to continue an agent live outside the model that proposes its next step?_

A single model invocation succeeds or fails on its own, but an autonomous agent runs across a horizon of many turns, and per-step errors compound with every turn. Over dozens of sequential tool interactions, a malformed call, a stale observation, or an unhandled exception can carry an unsupervised trajectory into a failure or a loop that no single step reveals. The agent harness is the runtime component that owns this loop: it schedules model calls, enforces the rules for moving between states, tracks task budgets, and holds sensitive actions for human approval. A model can be asked to pause, wait, or stay within an allowance, but a request it honors on almost every turn still fails across a long run, so the decision to continue must rest with deterministic supervision outside the model. Engineering the harness turns stochastic token generation into task execution that stays bounded, interruptible, and accountable across the whole horizon.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Design a runtime-owned trajectory record that tracks live plans, grants, consumption, and outstanding obligations
- Construct guarded state transitions that keep stale observations out of the next turn while preserving unresolved effects
- Calculate how long a control request waits for a turn boundary, and apply pause, cancel, or kill without dispatching incomplete output
- Explain which resources an asynchronous wait releases and which the trajectory still owns and pays for
- Design an approval gate with expiry and dispatch-time rechecks, and size the resources its held trajectories retain
- Allocate shared model-call service by weighted deficit round-robin while keeping provider quotas separate from trajectory budgets
- Apply bounded-liability admission before dispatch and select a budget ceiling by cost per accepted task

:::
## Supervising Continuation {#sec-vol3-harness-overview}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_h.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator triad with the Horizon axis highlighted."}

*The horizon exposure, bounded by a harness that keeps control outside the model.*
:::

Consider the connection-pool repair agent (lighthouse \ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}) at the moment it produces candidate patch `r18`. A test job is actively running against a fixed snapshot of that revision when an operator requests a pause for manual inspection. Simultaneously, an independent interactive task queues for model service, and the repair trajectory approaches its allocated budget. Even if the test job finishes cleanly and the next model reply is syntactically flawless, neither event answers whether the repair should proceed right now. That continuation decision depends on operational conditions outside the model: the operator's pending signal, current task states, shared cluster capacity, and the allowance remaining once in-flight work is accounted for.

The runtime components examined so far each address part of this operational environment. The tool layer tracks job handles and operation repeat contracts, the sandbox isolates execution and bounds workspace lifetimes, and the security checks test each dispatch against its confidentiality and provenance labels and bind each approval to the exact action it covers. Yet each of these mechanisms operates at the boundary of a single invocation, resource, or decision; none possesses the context or authority to decide whether the trajectory as a whole may take another step. That decision cannot be delegated to the model either. An agent instructed to self-regulate (to pause on request, or to halt before exceeding an allowance) evaluates that rule afresh on every turn. Because of horizon compounding (@eq-vol3-horizon-compounding), even a high per-turn compliance rate decays across an extended run, so a constraint the model honors on almost every turn is still violated in a predictable share of long trajectories. Furthermore, operational control requires state that cannot live in an ephemeral context window. An operator needs immediate status without reconstructing the conversation transcript; a scheduler must distinguish between work waiting on background jobs and work eligible to run; and the dispatch path must enforce security grants and token allowances before invoking downstream tools. All three operations demand a single, authoritative account of the trajectory that an unstructured message list cannot maintain.

The agent harness provides this missing supervisory layer by taking ownership of the execution loop for an individual trajectory. The agent proposes candidate actions; the harness determines whether each step runs immediately, yields to other work, or halts, and it enforces those decisions against an execution record that only the runtime can modify. This is trajectory-level encapsulation (principle \ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation}): the runtime governs each model call as one step of a whole trajectory, which advances only through transitions and admissions the runtime's guards permit, because the trajectory cannot be relied on to yield, to stop, or to notice that it has stopped making progress. Invariant closure (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}) says that bounds belong below the model; this principle names the unit those bounds must cover, the whole trajectory rather than the single call. The chapter turns it into two working rules. First, every outbound model call or tool dispatch must pass an explicit admission check (active operator signals, capability grants, shared capacity, and remaining budget) at the instant it would execute. Second, in-flight work stays accountable: no pause signal, timeout, or cancellation proves that running work has stopped or that its cost is settled, so every outstanding operation keeps a named owner until evidence settles it.

The harness develops in the order these decisions arise in one repair turn. The runtime first needs an authoritative account of the trajectory (@sec-vol3-controlplane-acb) and rules for how that account may change (@sec-vol3-controlplane-statemachine). Operators then need a way to stop or redirect it (@sec-vol3-controlplane-signals), and long tool jobs and human reviews need waits that keep supervision intact (@sec-vol3-controlplane-yielding, @sec-vol3-controlplane-hitl). Across many trajectories, shared model service must be divided (@sec-vol3-controlplane-scheduling), and across many turns, cumulative consumption must be bounded (@sec-vol3-controlplane-accounting). The record described here lives in host memory; making its guarantees survive host failure is the work of durable execution (@sec-vol3-durable-execution).

## The Loop and the Harness {#sec-vol3-controlplane-need}

When an autonomous agent runs inside a bare execution loop, an unexpected operator pause or an unconstrained retry cycle immediately exposes the lack of an external control plane: a path, separate from the one that performs model calls and tool work, that decides whether that work may proceed. An unmanaged loop treats model completions as direct execution instructions; a harness treats them as untrusted proposals, evaluating every action against explicit admission policies, budget constraints, and external supervisory signals.

### The anatomy of an unmanaged loop {#sec-vol3-harness-unmanaged-loop}

The unmediated while-loop of @lst-vol3-naive-agent-loop is the pattern most prototype agents still use, popularized by ReAct [@yao2023react]: invoke a foundation model, dispatch the tools requested in its completion, append the results to the message history, and repeat until the model emits a stopping condition. The introduction also divided a turn into six phases, from context assembly to assessment against the task contract, and observed that some phases wait on tools or people. What the loop lacks for production operation is a place for those phases' decisions to live. It confines all operational state to the message list and the local call stack of the client process.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The six-phase turn lifecycle, including the phases that pause a turn for tools and approvals, is established in @sec-vol3-intro-execution-lifecycle.
:::

Because an unmanaged loop lacks an independent, externally accessible control state, it cannot support the operational requirements of production systems. If an operator must pause an execution run while a long test suite executes, the runtime provides no interface to receive that command. If cumulative token consumption exhausts the allocated budget, the loop cannot withhold the next model call without terminating abruptly and abandoning in-flight work. Furthermore, any tool invocation proposed by the model executes immediately under ambient authority, bypassing policy checks or human review. Although a supervised harness may also execute as a loop or coroutine, it wraps that loop in an explicit state machine with invariant rules governing every continuation path, so that every proposal is filtered before any tool call is admitted (@fig-vol3-controlplane-arch).

::: {#fig-vol3-controlplane-arch fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The Prototype Loop vs. the Agent Harness**: Panel (a) runs the model's proposed call directly and keeps all state in the message list, so an outside request has nowhere to land, nothing bounds cumulative spend, and calls that policy would gate run at once. Panel (b) wraps the same loop in a harness whose trajectory record, guarded transitions, control and approval paths, and reserved budgets decide what is admitted. The model only proposes, and the tool layer settles the outcomes of admitted calls." fig-alt="Two stacked panels. The top panel shows a five-line while loop that calls a model, breaks on end_turn, runs the tool call, and appends the result, with comments reading no gate, no deadline and state lives only here, beside three boxes: cannot be stopped from outside, no ceiling on turns, tokens, or dollars, and gated calls run at once. The bottom panel shows a model box, a harness box, and a tools and sandbox box, joined by paired arrows labeled proposal and context, and admitted call and observation. The harness box lists trajectory record, guarded state transitions, control actions and approval gates, and budgets and ceilings."}

![](images/svg/fig-vol3-controlplane-arch.svg)

:::

In an unmanaged system, execution context is scattered across disparate subsystems: host operating systems track local processes, remote clusters hold asynchronous job handles, storage systems manage workspace leases, and identity providers track credential expirations. Panel (b) consolidates these responsibilities into a single runtime-owned record for each trajectory. Operators, cluster schedulers, and dispatch paths all consult this authoritative record before initiating state changes. While a system may pass budget constraints to the model in the prompt and the model may cooperate with pause requests, actual enforcement remains strictly with the runtime. Relying on model cooperation violates invariant closure; the runtime itself must guarantee that system safety invariants hold under all execution paths (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}).

::: {#dfn-agent-harness .callout-definition title="Agent harness"}

***Agent harness***\index{Agent harness!definition} is the runtime component that owns the agent loop for one trajectory, assembling each model call, interpreting the reply, deciding whether and when each proposed tool call is dispatched, and keeping the record through which outside components inspect, pause, bound, or stop continuation.

1. **Significance**: It keeps continuation decisions independent of model cooperation while preserving the grants, consumption, and outstanding work those decisions must respect.
2. **Distinction**: The tool layer mediates calls and tracks their outcomes, and the sandbox bounds execution under its policy. The harness composes those mechanisms with control requests, waiting, scheduling, and lifetime budgets.
3. **Common pitfall**: Keeping status and pending obligations only in prompt text or inaccessible execution-local state, so a separate control path cannot inspect them or prevent further dispatch.

:::

### One turn under supervision {#sec-vol3-harness-lifecycle-turn}

A software repair workflow illustrates how this division of labor operates in practice. @Tbl-vol3-harness-control-trace traces an illustrative sequence of events around a single execution turn, from the moment the repair becomes eligible for another model call, through the model's proposal to run the regression test against candidate `r18`, to the operator's resume. The cells describe each decision in plain terms; the sections that follow supply the mechanism behind each one. The lifecycle states record whether the trajectory is eligible for continuation (`READY`), actively querying the model (`CALLING_MODEL`), awaiting tool completion (`WAITING_TOOL`), or suspended by an operator (`PAUSED`).

| Event                                             | Harness decision and recorded obligation                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|:--------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| The repair is eligible for another model call     | From `READY`, confirm that no operator request is pending, that shared model capacity is available, and that the budget covers the most this call could cost. Set that amount aside, then enter `CALLING_MODEL` and send the call |
| A complete reply proposes the test of `r18`       | Record what the call actually used. Check the proposed test against the task's permissions and the remaining budget, set aside the test's maximum cost, and record the test as running before sending it. Enter `WAITING_TOOL`    |
| The operator requests a pause while the test runs | Stop admitting new work. Keep tracking the running test and its cost, but no longer let its result restart the model; then step through `READY` to `PAUSED` with no moment at which new work could start                          |
| The test result arrives during the pause          | Confirm that the result is genuine and belongs to this test of `r18`. Record its outcome and cost, but leave the trajectory paused and the model's context unchanged                                                              |
| The operator requests resume                      | Recheck task state, permissions, the recorded evidence, and the budget before returning to `READY`. The scheduler may then admit another call; the result supports only the test and revision it actually checked                 |

: **A repair trajectory under supervision**: An illustrative control trace. A paused trajectory admits no new work, yet its outstanding job and charges keep an owner. {#tbl-vol3-harness-control-trace}

Three features of the trace recur through the rest of the chapter. First, every row that admits work reserves before it sends. Affordability cannot be judged from settled charges alone, because the running test job may still bill and the proposed call may generate up to its full output allowance; the harness therefore reserves each operation's worst-case liability at admission and reconciles reported usage afterward. Notebook \ref{nbk-10-bounded-liability-admission} later prices a call that a check of settled spend admits and this reservation test refuses. Second, the pause and the test result are independent events. The pause stops new admission without stopping the job, and the job's result settles its ledger entry without resuming the turn. Third, the reply's content never acts on its own: a truncated or canceled reply yields nothing to dispatch, a claim of completion triggers an independent check rather than ending the task, and an action that policy requires a human to review waits in a dedicated hold with its own expiry. Each of these needs runtime state that the message list does not have.

The trace also separates the decision to continue from the resources an agent holds. While the repair trajectory sits in `PAUSED` or `WAITING_TOOL`, it keeps its workspace, its cached repository state, and its running test job, but it does not hold a worker thread or a place in the queue for model calls. Because the harness, not the repair loop, decides when the trajectory next calls the model, an interactive trajectory can take the next model-call slot without waiting for the repair to give it up. Which resources a wait releases, and which it keeps, is the subject of supervised waiting (@sec-vol3-controlplane-yielding); how model calls are divided among trajectories is the subject of scheduling (@sec-vol3-controlplane-scheduling).

## The Trajectory Record {#sec-vol3-controlplane-acb}

When an operator issues a pause request, the conversation transcript cannot answer the questions the harness must resolve. The transcript records what the user and model said, but runtime decisions require knowing the state of the underlying system: which candidate revision is under test, whether a background validation job has finished, how much compute budget remains once outstanding asynchronous tasks are accounted for, and whether any external side effects are still in flight. Simultaneously, the cluster scheduler must distinguish a trajectory blocked on a container execution from one actively waiting for its next inference turn. None of these operational facts belong in the prompt. Resolving them requires runtime-owned control state that the harness can inspect, mutate, and enforce directly without relying on the foundation model to reconstruct its own execution history.

::: {#dfn-trajectory-record .callout-definition title="Trajectory record"}

***Trajectory record***\index{Trajectory record!definition} is the per-trajectory control state owned and maintained by the harness. It encapsulates identity and task scope, lifecycle state, resource limits and financial accounting, security grants and workspace leases, pending asynchronous operations, and references to prompt context, the live execution plan, container environments, and verified evidence.

1. **Significance**: It provides the harness with an authoritative, centralized structure to inspect and govern the entire trajectory, tracking resource consumption, pending asynchronous operations, and security grants across inference calls.
2. **Distinction**: While the conversation transcript records user-model message exchanges, the trajectory record tracks the operational state required to govern execution across multiple turns. Furthermore, a live in-memory record represents active control state, not a durable audit log or proof that external claims are verified.
3. **Common pitfall**: Treating a model's generated text or self-reported progress as an authoritative update to consumed budget, granted capabilities, tool execution results, or task completion.

:::

@Tbl-vol3-acb-schema organizes these fields by the supervisory decisions they support. In practice, this structure represents a logical schema: a distributed runtime may partition these field groups across different storage backends, for example keeping ephemeral context references in memory while persisting financial ledgers to an external store, provided each group retains a single authoritative writer and a well-defined update protocol.

| Field group                         | Contents                                                                                                       | Supervisory use                                                                       |
|:------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Identity and task                   | Trajectory, requester, tenant, optional parent, task contract and version                                      | Bind requests and charges to the right task and authority                             |
| Control                             | `state`, `record_version`, `control_epoch`, `pending_control`, exit reason                                     | Decide whether a continuation or state change is current and permitted                |
| Continuation                        | Context reference and version, live-plan reference and revision, candidate workspace and evidence references   | Assemble the next call from the intended task state                                   |
| Limits and accounting               | Per-call limits, `actual_consumption`, `outstanding_reservations`, `finalization_reserve`, and `deadline`      | Check new liability against the remaining allowance and preserve funds for final work |
| Authority and resources             | Current grants, workspace leases, credential-broker references, resource owners                                | Check accessible operations and identify resources requiring release or transfer      |
| Current invocation and observations | `current_model_call`, `observation_eligible_calls`, attempt IDs, job handles, deadlines, and expected versions | Correlate events and decide which may inform the current continuation                 |
| Held approval                       | `held_approval`: exact proposal reference, applicable task and plan versions, approval status and expiry       | Keep a proposed action undispatched while its decision is pending                     |
| Outstanding obligations             | `operation_ledger` reference, unresolved outcomes and charges, settlement owner                                | Preserve responsibility after a timeout, plan revision, pause, or scheduling exit     |

: **Trajectory Record Fields**: Each field group supports a control decision; references preserve access to larger state without implying that the referenced resources are free or absent. {#tbl-vol3-acb-schema}

Two questions about a running operation must be answered separately: whether its result may still inform the model, and whether the harness still owes anything for it. The first is **observation eligibility**\index{Observation eligibility!definition}, which defines whether the output of an operation is permitted to enter the prompt context for the next model invocation. The second is an outstanding obligation, and the two can come apart. A tool call can lose observation eligibility (when an invocation step times out, or the user cancels a subtask) even while the remote execution continues running in a backend container. To prevent orphaned side effects and resource leaks, the **operation ledger**\index{Operation ledger!definition} tracks every logical operation across its entire lifecycle: transport retries, incoming execution evidence, and the specific subsystem responsible for final settlement.

The trajectory record manages this lifecycle through two versioning counters. While `record_version` increments on every serialized update to provide optimistic concurrency control, the **control epoch**\index{Control epoch!definition} (`control_epoch`) tracks the specific planning and invocation cycle against which proposals and observations are validated. The epoch does not advance on every turn; it advances when the harness withdraws a continuation's claim on outstanding results, as when a wait deadline expires, an operator interrupts, or a plan revision supersedes pending work. Each call records the epoch current at its registration, so an ordinary result from this turn's dispatch still matches. Incrementing the epoch invalidates in-flight observations registered under the earlier epoch without breaking the underlying operation's idempotency contract. As a result, the harness continues tracking background tasks and their external side effects even after the agent has stopped waiting for their immediate output.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The operation idempotency contract and retry semantics are established in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency.
:::

A parallel discipline governs resource accounting. The harness separates settled usage (`actual_consumption`) from provisional allocations (`outstanding_reservations`), which represent admitted operations whose compute or financial costs have not yet been finalized. The harness withholds a dedicated **finalization reserve**\index{Finalization reserve!definition} from general exploratory steps. This reserve guarantees that the runtime retains sufficient budget to execute mandated cleanup tasks, release sandboxes, and run deterministic verification suites before the trajectory terminates. Wall-clock deadlines operate independently of token limits, because waiting on remote containers or human reviewers consumes real time even when token generation is idle. @Sec-vol3-controlplane-accounting formalizes this admission test; the trajectory record provides the live metrics required to enforce it.

These lifecycle and accounting guarantees unite under one working rule, the *settlement rule*. It is the trajectory-level form of settlement before retry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement}). That principle says a timeout does not establish whether an effect occurred, so a blind retry is unsafe; the settlement rule adds that losing interest in a result does not release the effect's charge or its owner either. Under this rule, withdrawing an operation's observation eligibility, whether through a timeout, a plan revision, an operator pause, or trajectory cancellation, never clears the operation or refunds its financial reservation from the ledger. Only authenticated, correlated evidence can settle an outcome, confirm completion, or release reserved budget. Until that proof arrives, the outstanding obligation retains a designated settlement owner responsible for reconciling its ultimate state.

### Update authority and referenced state {#sec-vol3-agent-harness-update-authority}

Only the harness possesses write authority over the trajectory record. While the model can propose plan changes, tool calls, or completion assertions, the harness treats these outputs strictly as unverified proposals. Each update must pass admission checks before the runtime commits it to the record. Provider billing APIs and tool execution metrics supply authoritative consumption figures, cryptographically signed or authenticated tool events supply operational evidence, and control APIs supply verified operator intent. Decoupling this control plane from prompt text ensures strict enforceability: an agent may receive read-only notifications of its remaining budget, but it can never manipulate the meter.

To keep control operations lightweight and prevent multi-megabyte state copies during routine scheduler queries, the trajectory record stores references (content hashes, storage URIs, and job identifiers) rather than deep-copying full prompt contexts, workspace filesystems, or observation payloads. However, these references represent real underlying resource commitments. A paused or waiting trajectory continues to consume resources across distributed subsystems: KV-cache allocations in inference engines, isolated container environments and disk volumes, and open network sockets. The trajectory record holds the authoritative handles to these external assets and signals lifecycle transitions to their respective managers.

All mechanisms discussed in this section assume an active in-memory host. Preserving this control state across process crashes and ensuring that record updates remain strictly serialized with respect to external side effects requires write-ahead logging and durable execution protocols. A dedicated durable-log offset in the control record binds the volatile runtime state to its persistent backing log.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Committing each admitted operation and its reservation to durable storage before dispatch is developed in @sec-vol3-persistence-wal.
:::

### The live plan {#sec-vol3-harness-live-plan}

While test-time compute strategies use dependency graphs over candidate artifacts to explore solutions, runtime execution demands a **live plan**\index{Live plan!definition}. A live plan is a dependency-ordered directed acyclic graph of execution steps that explicitly separates proposed actions from operations currently in flight and evidence already verified. Each step in the plan defines a unique identifier, explicit prerequisite steps or evidence dependencies, the target candidate artifact and operating conditions to which it applies, and its current execution status. When the harness admits a step, it binds that step directly to an entry in the operation ledger. Similarly, when a step completes, the harness links it to the immutable evidence supporting that completion, never to an unverified checkbox emitted in model text.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
⇄ **Contrast:** The revisable candidate plan established in @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-planning-revision tracks only unexecuted candidate operations and their supporting evidence; the live plan also records operations in flight.
:::

Consider a practical software repair workflow where candidate `r18` has just been generated. The live plan differentiates between the source edit that produced candidate `r18`, the targeted unit test running against that specific revision, and the broader integration suite required by the task contract. While the test runner executes in a background container, the plan records the step as in-flight rather than optimistically assuming success. When the test runner completes, a passing status validates only that targeted test against candidate `r18` under those exact container flags; the remaining verification steps and final acceptance criteria remain unfulfilled. An operator's pause request arriving mid-test acts as an independent supervisory event, interrupting further dispatch without corrupting the historical inputs or the validity of the ongoing test execution.

When incoming observations demonstrate that a strategy is failing, the model may propose a plan revision to alter downstream tasks. Before adopting any revised plan, the harness validates it against the overarching task contract, current evidence dependencies, remaining budget, and security grants. Adopting the revision advances the plan revision counter and invalidates pending, undispatched proposals and held approvals whose underlying assumptions have changed. Existing verified evidence remains valid under its original operating conditions. The harness synchronizes plan adoption with the tool dispatcher to prevent race conditions where a stale proposal might pass admission against a superseded plan.

Now consider what happens if a plan revision modifies the source code while the targeted test for candidate `r18` is still running in the background. The active container job is testing candidate `r18`, not the new revision. Relabeling the step in the plan cannot convert those eventual test results into evidence for the modified code. Furthermore, deleting the step from the plan does not abort the remote job, reverse its external side effects, or automatically refund its compute reservation. Instead, the harness preserves the active operation in the ledger under its original settlement owner, blocks downstream steps whose prerequisites are no longer satisfied, and evaluates the replacement work through a fresh admission check. In robust systems, recovering from external operations requires explicit compensation and failure-handling logic rather than retroactively editing plan text.

By maintaining an explicit, dependency-tracked live plan, the trajectory record delineates what the agent has proposed, what the harness has admitted to the execution plane, and what obligations remain outstanding. Preserving consistency across concurrent tool events, asynchronous worker callbacks, and operator interruptions requires the harness to strictly govern how this record evolves, binding all lifecycle mutations to formal, guarded state transitions.

## Trajectory States {#sec-vol3-controlplane-statemachine}

Consider an automated software repair trajectory that submits a suite of test cases for candidate `r18`. If the wait deadline elapses before a result arrives, the harness must record the outcome as unknown and proceed. One minute later, the test service returns a success report. Both statements reflect reality: the outcome was indeed unknown when the deadline expired, and the tests ultimately passed. The failure occurs if the harness splices that late result into an obsolete turn as though the model had possessed the evidence when selecting its next action. This defect, known as **observation crossing**\index{Observation crossing!definition}, conflates the asynchronous physical history of an operation with the causal evidence admitted to a particular continuation. Preventing it takes two pieces developed in this section: guarded transitions that decide when a continuation may advance, and an epoch fence that decides which late results may still inform it (@sec-vol3-agent-harness-late-results).

A state machine with guarded transitions[^fn-guarded-transition-statecharts] makes every such admission explicit. Beyond resolving observation races, guarded transitions prevent scheduling anomalies, such as mistaking a trajectory held for human approval as idle and erroneously dispatching another model call. The runtime control plane, rather than generated model output, governs all state transitions. @Tbl-vol3-lifecycle-states defines this supervisory state machine, organized around five live states, a finalizing state through which every exit must pass, and three terminal absorbing outcomes.

[^fn-guarded-transition-statecharts]: **Guarded Transition**: Harel's statecharts [@harel1987] labeled each transition with the event that triggers it and a condition that must hold for it to fire, and added hierarchy and concurrency so that reactive controllers stayed readable as their state counts grew. The harness uses the flat core of that formalism: an event proposes an edge, and the guard, evaluated against the record at that moment, decides whether it fires. Keeping the guard on the edge, rather than in whichever handler happens to receive the event, is what lets one table govern every path into `CALLING_MODEL`. \index{Statecharts!guarded transitions}

| State                             | Meaning                                                                                  | Legal next states                                          |
|:----------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------|
| `READY`                           | Eligible to be considered for the next model call; admission guards still apply.         | `CALLING_MODEL`, `PAUSED`, `FINALIZING`                    |
| `CALLING_MODEL`                   | A model invocation is registered for the current continuation.                           | `READY`, `WAITING_TOOL`, `AWAITING_APPROVAL`, `FINALIZING` |
| `WAITING_TOOL`                    | The continuation awaits a declared set or batch of tool observations.                    | `READY`, `FINALIZING`                                      |
| `AWAITING_APPROVAL`               | An exact proposed action is held; approval and dispatch eligibility remain unresolved.   | `WAITING_TOOL`, `READY`, `FINALIZING`                      |
| `PAUSED`                          | The continuation is held at a local boundary; no new model or tool work is admitted.     | `READY`, `FINALIZING`                                      |
| `FINALIZING`                      | The runtime is checking the exit outcome and resolving or transferring remaining duties. | `COMPLETED`, `FAILED`, `CANCELED`                          |
| `COMPLETED`, `FAILED`, `CANCELED` | The continuation has ended; retained evidence and assigned obligations may remain.       | None                                                       |

: **Guarded Trajectory States**: An edge permits consideration of a transition, not unconditional execution. Events can update accounting or evidence without changing state. {#tbl-vol3-lifecycle-states}

The normal operational cycle follows `READY` → `CALLING_MODEL` → `WAITING_TOOL` → `READY`, tracing through the five live states and guarded transitions shown in @fig-vol3-harness-trajectory-states: proposals requiring review divert into `AWAITING_APPROVAL`, pause commands transition to `PAUSED` exclusively from `READY`, and all termination triggers (completion requests, cancellations, or exhausted budgets) route through `FINALIZING` before reaching absorbing terminal states (`COMPLETED`, `FAILED`, `CANCELED`). During execution, a model response may produce no admissible action, request task completion, or propose an action requiring operator approval. While the normalized invocation status defined in @tbl-vol3-invocation-status fixes how the runtime processes individual call outcomes, @tbl-vol3-harness-status-routing specifies how each outcome shifts the overall trajectory state. Two names appear in both vocabularies with different meanings: a reply status of `COMPLETED` or `CANCELED` describes one model call, while the terminal states of the same names describe the whole trajectory. A completed reply ends a call, not the task. Only a reply whose status is `COMPLETED` proceeds to tool candidate validation. The harness must never convert a malformed, truncated, or canceled partial stream into an actionable tool invocation simply because a parser managed to salvage partial arguments from the payload.

| Reply status and content               | Next state          | Condition or residue                                                          |
|:---------------------------------------|:--------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `COMPLETED`, validated tool proposal   | `WAITING_TOOL`      | Once its dispatch is admitted                                                 |
| `COMPLETED`, proposal requiring review | `AWAITING_APPROVAL` | When policy requires review of the exact action                               |
| `COMPLETED`, completion request        | `FINALIZING`        | The task's completion check follows                                           |
| `COMPLETED`, no admissible action      | `READY`             | With an observation saying so                                                 |
| `TRUNCATED`, `REFUSED`, `REJECTED`     | `READY`             | With a bounded observation, unless the task's refusal policy finalizes        |
| `CANCELED`                             | `READY`             | Under the control hold that caused the cancellation                           |
| `TRANSPORT_FAILURE`, `FAULTED`         | `READY`             | For bounded failure handling while the budget permits, `FINALIZING` otherwise |

: **Reply Status and Next State**: Every non-completed status returns to a state that admits no dispatch from the failed reply; reservations for failed or faulted calls stay outstanding until usage settles. {#tbl-vol3-harness-status-routing tbl-colwidths="[34,20,46]"}

Action approval introduces a controlled detour to this cycle. An approved action transitions from `AWAITING_APPROVAL` to `WAITING_TOOL` only when its active dispatch guards pass; recording operator approval does not automatically execute the tool. Conversely, a denial, expiration, or operator withdrawal emits a refusal observation back to `READY`.

::: {#fig-vol3-harness-trajectory-states fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Trajectory State Machine**: Five live states, a finalizing state, and three terminal outcomes. The ordinary cycle runs from READY through CALLING_MODEL and WAITING_TOOL back to READY; a proposal that policy requires reviewed is held in AWAITING_APPROVAL, and pause is entered only from READY. Every exit passes through FINALIZING, which stops admission and resolves or transfers remaining duties before an absorbing terminal state. Each arrow is a guarded edge, and events such as a late result or a usage report can update the record's ledger without changing state." fig-alt="State diagram with a live-states region and an exit region. Live states PAUSED, READY, CALLING_MODEL, WAITING_TOOL, and AWAITING_APPROVAL are connected by labeled arrows: pause and resume, call admitted, no admissible action, tool call admitted, approval required by policy, approved and guards pass, wait policy met, and a dashed arrow for denied, expired, or stale requests back to READY. A completion request arrow and a dashed arrow from any live state for cancel, kill, or a budget or deadline stop lead to FINALIZING, which leads to COMPLETED, FAILED, and CANCELED."}

![](images/svg/harness-trajectory-states.svg)

:::

### Transition guards and the admission check {#sec-vol3-agent-harness-transition-guards}

Navigating a legal edge in the state machine is merely a necessary condition for progress, not an unconditional entitlement to execute. Before the runtime admits new work, whether invoking a model or dispatching a tool, it evaluates a comprehensive set of predicates known as the *admission check*. This check enforces several simultaneous invariants: no pending control holds may exist; the active context, credentials, and required action approvals must remain valid; upstream data dependencies must be resolved; and adequate deadline slack and downstream service capacity must be confirmed. Furthermore, the runtime must reserve the operation's bounded financial liability from the task budget without encroaching on the dedicated finalization reserve (@sec-vol3-controlplane-accounting). For tool calls, the admission check also verifies that arguments are structurally complete. Because system state evolves continuously, this evaluation holds only for the instant it executes. An approval granted seconds earlier or a scheduling decision made on a previous tick does not carry forward; if an unresolved prior operation blocks a dependent mutation, the trajectory cannot dispatch that mutation even if it remains in `READY` for independent work.

The admission check and its state updates execute as a single atomic transaction. Protected by the trajectory record lock,[^fn-record-lock-monitor] the harness evaluates the guard predicates, reserves the required liability, registers the outgoing invocation or attempt ID, marks the expected observation as eligible, and commits the state transition. After releasing the record lock, the runtime passes the admitted request to a release gate that serializes the final release-or-withhold decision with control updates. This gate rechecks current controls and the existing admission without reserving liability twice; slow network I/O remains outside the record lock. This design enforces the *register-before-send rule*. Registering state prior to dispatch ensures that ultra-low-latency responses never arrive before the local record exists to receive them. Conversely, transmitting requests strictly outside the critical section prevents slow network I/O, stalled inference endpoints, or lagging tool services from blocking concurrent control actions, scheduler ticks, or arriving results from other workers.

[^fn-record-lock-monitor]: **Record Lock as a Monitor**: Hoare's monitors [@hoare1974monitors] bundled shared data with the only procedures allowed to touch it and ran those procedures one at a time, so every invariant on the data could be checked at procedure entry and exit. The trajectory record is a monitor in this sense: controllers, schedulers, and result handlers all reach it through short guarded procedures. The register-before-send rule adds one constraint for a record whose procedures front slow remote services: no procedure waits on a model or tool call while holding the lock. \index{Monitor!trajectory record}

Because external control requests acquire this same monitor lock, stops and admissions are strictly serialized. This sequencing establishes the *admission-order rule*. If a pause, cancellation, or kill command commits before an admission check runs, it immediately blocks new outbound work. Conversely, if admission commits first, the operation becomes owned work with a registered identity and reservation. A later control cannot erase that record or refund its liability on intent alone. The release gate can still withhold a definitely unsent attempt, but settlement requires authoritative evidence that release did not occur and that no remote liability remains. Once release may have occurred, a cancellation request cannot establish `not_sent`; remote evidence must settle the outcome. A volatile withheld flag alone cannot establish non-release after a host crash. Tool-side idempotency and stale-lease fencing still require the endpoint contracts detailed in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-operation-ids.

To coordinate concurrent state access without heavyweight distributed locks, the harness pairs optimistic concurrency validation with epoch fencing. The `record_version` field detects competing updates at the point of commit, implementing the validation step of optimistic concurrency control [@kung1981optimistic]. In parallel, increments to `control_epoch` fence out stale asynchronous responses\index{Control epoch!fencing}, the same generation-number check that the tool layer applies to superseded workers at the endpoint. Here the fenced party is an observation: a response stamped with an old epoch cannot advance the current continuation, however well formed it is. These control plane identifiers operate alongside, rather than replace, logical operation identifiers and transport attempt counters. A network retry generates a new attempt ID under the same logical operation, whereas an operator interruption bumps the control epoch to invalidate pending replies without erasing the operation's accounting ledger.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Epoch fencing of superseded workers at the mutating resource is established in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-operation-ids.
:::

The record now carries several counters, and each advances on different events and rejects a different kind of stale input (@tbl-vol3-harness-counters).

| Counter               | Advances when                                                                                                      | What a stale value rejects                                                 |
|:----------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `record_version`      | Any committed update to the trajectory record                                                                      | A decision made on a view of the record that has since changed             |
| `control_epoch`       | A wait deadline, an operator interrupt, or a plan revision withdraws a continuation's claim on outstanding results | A result registered under an earlier epoch, as input to the current turn   |
| Plan revision         | The harness adopts a revised live plan                                                                             | A proposal or held approval formed against the superseded plan             |
| Held-proposal version | The harness records a new or changed held proposal for approval (@sec-vol3-controlplane-hitl)                      | An approval decision for a different version of the proposal               |
| Attempt ID            | A transport retry of the same logical operation                                                                    | Nothing by itself; it lets late evidence name the attempt that produced it |

: **Trajectory Record Counters**: Each counter advances on its own events and rejects its own kind of stale input, so none can stand in for another. {#tbl-vol3-harness-counters tbl-colwidths="[20,42,38]"}

@Lst-vol3-guarded-transition expresses these rules as a single supervisory procedure. The legal edges match @tbl-vol3-lifecycle-states, and any edge without a registered guard predicate is rejected by default. The caller provides the `record_version` it observed when formulating its transition request; a concurrent modification by another worker causes the version check to fail. Similarly, duplicate deliveries of an event fail either the version check or the edge guard, guaranteeing that no action is admitted twice.

::: {#lst-vol3-guarded-transition lst-cap="**Guarded Transitions**: Every state change checks the legal edge, its explicit guard, and the record version under the record lock, then performs admission bookkeeping before the state changes; the admitted request is sent only after the lock is released."}
```python
LIVE = {"READY", "CALLING_MODEL", "WAITING_TOOL",
        "AWAITING_APPROVAL", "PAUSED"}
LEGAL = {("READY", "CALLING_MODEL"), ("READY", "PAUSED"),
         ("CALLING_MODEL", "READY"), ("CALLING_MODEL", "WAITING_TOOL"),
         ("CALLING_MODEL", "AWAITING_APPROVAL"), ("WAITING_TOOL", "READY"),
         ("AWAITING_APPROVAL", "WAITING_TOOL"),
         ("AWAITING_APPROVAL", "READY"), ("PAUSED", "READY")}
LEGAL |= {(s, "FINALIZING") for s in LIVE}
LEGAL |= {("FINALIZING", t) for t in ("COMPLETED", "FAILED", "CANCELED")}
# GUARDS maps each edge to a predicate over (record, decision).

def transition(rec, new_state, decision, admit=None):
    with rec.lock:                            # the local decision only
        edge = (rec.state, new_state)
        guard = GUARDS.get(edge)              # no guard, no permission
        if edge not in LEGAL or guard is None or not guard(rec, decision):
            raise IllegalTransition(edge, decision.id)
        if decision.seen_version != rec.record_version:
            raise StaleDecision(decision.id)  # a competing update won
        if admit is not None:
            admit(rec)                        # reserve, register, set eligibility
        rec.state = new_state
        rec.record_version += 1
        rec.history.append((edge, decision.id, rec.record_version))
    # The caller passes admitted work to the serialized release gate outside this lock.
```
:::

Here, the guard registered on the `READY` → `CALLING_MODEL` edge executes the complete admission check, while `admit` performs the liability reservations and bookkeeping required by the register-before-send rule. Because the monitor lock protects only in-memory lookups, state updates, and an array append, lock contention remains negligible compared to the hundreds of milliseconds consumed by remote inference or tool execution.

### Late results and observation eligibility {#sec-vol3-agent-harness-late-results}

When an asynchronous tool result arrives, the harness must reconcile financial and physical state without corrupting the prompt history of an active turn. Upon reception, the runtime authenticates the payload and correlates its task identifier, logical operation ID, and attempt number against the trajectory record. Mismatched or unauthenticated messages are logged for audit and dropped. Valid results immediately update the trajectory's persistent ledger: the runtime records raw execution evidence and converts reserved financial liabilities into settled resource usage.

However, updating the operational ledger does not imply that the result belongs in the model's current prompt context. As demonstrated in @lst-vol3-harness-on-result, the runtime splits incoming evidence into two separate paths: universal ledger settlement and epoch-fenced observation staging. While every authentic result records evidence and settles any confirmed usage, an observation is staged for immediate prompt injection only if its call ID remains registered in `observation_eligible_calls` and the epoch recorded with the call at registration matches the active `control_epoch`. The remote service never sees the epoch; when the harness correlates the result, it looks up the epoch by call ID and attaches it to the local result envelope as `result.epoch`. This field comes from the registration record, not the remote payload. The two checks fail in different ways. The eligibility set is the per-call statement of which results the current wait expects, and removing an entry after staging is what stops a redelivery from being staged twice. The epoch is a bulk fence: a timeout or operator interrupt advances it once and thereby invalidates every call registered under the old epoch, including any whose removal from the set was missed. If an operation timed out or an operator intervened, its recorded epoch is obsolete. The harness settles the financial balance but refuses to inject the result into the current turn, which eliminates observation crossing. Should that late evidence prove relevant to future turns, the runtime can re-evaluate and stage it during subsequent guarded context assembly. Staging a result does not by itself end the wait. A declared **wait policy**\index{Wait policy!definition} establishes the criteria required to return from `WAITING_TOOL` to `READY`, and the handler requests that transition only when the policy is satisfied.

::: {#lst-vol3-harness-on-result lst-cap="**Routing a Tool Result**: Authenticated evidence always reaches the operation ledger and settles usage, while only a currently eligible result under the current control epoch is staged for the waiting continuation."}
```python
def on_tool_result(rec, result):
    if not authenticate(result):
        return audit(rec, "unauthenticated_result", result)
    with rec.lock:
        op = rec.operation_ledger.get(result.operation_id)
        if op is None or result.attempt_id not in op.attempts:
            return audit(rec, "unknown_operation", result)
        if not op.record_evidence(result):  # already recorded: duplicate
            return
        settle(rec, op, result.usage)       # reserved -> actual; rest stays owed
        eligible = (result.call_id in rec.observation_eligible_calls
                    and result.epoch == rec.control_epoch)
        if eligible:
            rec.observation_eligible_calls.discard(result.call_id)
            stage_observation(rec, result)  # for the current wait only
        rec.record_version += 1
        seen = rec.record_version
    if eligible and wait_policy_satisfied(rec):  # the guard rechecks it
        transition(rec, "READY", Decision(result.id, seen))
```
:::

Systems typically implement one of four wait policies: all required results arrive, an acceptable partial batch completes, a wait deadline expires, or an operator triggers an explicit withdrawal. The trajectory record carefully distinguishes confirmed evidence from unreturned, unresolved calls. In the candidate `r18` repair scenario, a timeout records that the outcome was unknown at the deadline; it cannot justify inferring that the test suite failed. When the test service eventually reports that candidate `r18` passed, the ledger records that verified outcome with its exact scope. Furthermore, a timeout never authorizes an uncoordinated re-execution of a non-idempotent operation. Dependent actions must still satisfy all guard preconditions and adhere to the tool's mutation safety contract.

### Pause entry and outstanding work {#sec-vol3-agent-harness-pause-entry}

To maintain a clean supervisory contract, the state machine permits entry into `PAUSED` exclusively from `READY`. If a pause command arrives while the trajectory is in `CALLING_MODEL` or `WAITING_TOOL`, the runtime cannot abruptly discard the state of remote interactions. Instead, it asserts a `pending_control` hold, which prevents the admission of any subsequent work. The harness revokes observation eligibility for active model streams, invalidates any pending approval requests, and terminates the active observation wait; for a trajectory in `WAITING_TOOL`, this is the explicit-withdrawal wait policy, and it is what permits the `WAITING_TOOL` → `READY` step. If policy dictates, the control plane issues cancellation requests to remote workers; under the settlement rule, these operations remain registered in the ledger until remote confirmation arrives. Any partial token stream received from a canceled model call is preserved solely for diagnostic logging, never stitched together to form a valid dispatch.

Once these local eligibility revocations are logged, the trajectory steps through `READY` directly into `PAUSED` under the existing admission hold. Because the lock prevents concurrent scheduling during this step-down, no runnable window opens between the transitions. Entering `PAUSED` halts continuation progress, ensuring that neither pending responses nor held proposals can advance the continuation. However, background tools already running in external systems may continue their physical execution. For example, the remote test execution for candidate `r18` can complete while the trajectory remains paused; its completion payload updates the ledger and settles liability without triggering a new inference cycle.

Resuming execution requires a guarded `PAUSED` → `READY` transition, followed by a brand-new admission check that reconciles all ledger evidence accumulated during the pause. Resumption is not an automated rollback of pause-time revocations; state withdrawn during a pause is never restored. Expired authorization tokens remain expired, withdrawn approvals require fresh operator authorization, and canceled partial responses are permanently abandoned. If an earlier operation remains unconfirmed, its unresolved state continues to block dependent actions even if unrelated steps are eligible. Meanwhile, physical resource retention operates under independent lifecycles: sandboxed workspace leases, buffer allocations, compute reservations, and model context caches persist or expire according to their respective lifetime policies rather than the trajectory's instantaneous state.

### Finalization and remaining duties {#sec-vol3-agent-harness-finalization-duties}

Every exit path passes through `FINALIZING`. Upon entering this state, the runtime immediately suspends standard work admission, records the exit reason, revokes unused delegation authority where supported, and triggers the task completion check when completion is claimed. An end-of-turn token emitted by a model merely requests this validation; genuine task completion requires an independent completion check, such as the task contract's acceptance tests, run outside the model. All finalization checks and mandatory cleanup routines draw from their dedicated, pre-funded reserve.

During finalization, the control plane may block to await pending results, report verification failures, or hand off outstanding cancellation, billing reconciliation, and resource reclamation tasks to an external supervisor. The transition guard into any terminal state requires that every outstanding obligation be either definitively settled or explicitly transferred to an accepting upstream owner. Simply clearing an unresolved task from a local tracking set violates the guard. To effect a legitimate transfer, the runtime must transmit complete metadata (operation IDs, ledger evidence, and funding allocations), allowing the recipient service to assume supervisory responsibility.

All terminal states (`COMPLETED`, `FAILED`, and `CANCELED`) are strictly absorbing. Once a trajectory enters a terminal state, its continuation terminates permanently. Late-arriving tool results or ledger settlements can still update archived historical records through the designated supervisory owner, but no event can transition the continuation back to `READY`. Resuming an investigation or re-attempting a task requires instantiating a fresh trajectory with a new identifier linked back to the prior run. Within this architecture, `COMPLETED` denotes solely that the programmatic completion criteria configured for the harness were met. Whether those criteria demonstrate true task competence is an empirical systems question addressed in @sec-vol3-evaluation-problem.

::: {#chk-10-agent-control-block .callout-checkpoint title="Trajectory record and guarded states"}

- [ ] **Late test evidence**: The wait for `r18` times out, then a success result arrives during `PAUSED`. Decide which structure changes, `observation_eligible_calls` or the `operation_ledger`, and name the guarded step that must run before the next model call can use the result.
- [ ] **Pause boundary**: Write the sequence of record updates that takes `WAITING_TOOL` through `READY` to `PAUSED`. At which point is new admission blocked, and which entries stay in the ledger?
- [ ] **Admission race**: Two schedulers both read `record_version` 41 and try to admit a model call. Using @lst-vol3-guarded-transition, which check rejects the loser, and what has the loser reserved or sent by then?
- [ ] **Terminal responsibility**: Cancellation of a paid job is unconfirmed when the continuation ends. List what the terminal guard requires before `CANCELED`, and who owns the job's charge afterward.

:::

Guarded transitions keep every update to the record causally consistent under network delays, tool timeouts, and concurrent interventions. They describe pause entry, however, only from the record's side. An operator who presses pause needs more: an authenticated way to register the request, a bound on how long it takes effect while a model call is still generating, and a distinction between a pause, a cancellation, and a kill that leaves outstanding work owned in each case.

## Control Actions {#sec-vol3-controlplane-signals}

The test job for candidate `r18` is still executing when an operator requests a pause. The harness must halt the repair loop's forward progress without losing the job's tracking identity, its allocated budget reservation, or the diagnostic evidence it might return. Delaying the pause until the test finishes strips the operator of interactive control over potentially runaway execution. Conversely, declaring the job canceled merely because the trajectory state transitions to `PAUSED` fabricates an execution outcome the runtime has not yet observed.

External control decouples receiving a request from establishing the physical execution state that request demands. When an operator intervenes, the harness authenticates the caller, verifies authority over the target trajectory, and appends the requested directive to `pending_control` while holding the record lock. Because this update occurs under the lock, the admission-ordering invariants established in @sec-vol3-controlplane-statemachine fix exactly which operations fall under the request's scope. The controller acknowledges the hold to the operator only after the update commits to the record (and, once durable execution is in place, to its log). Furthermore, the response delivered to the operator must distinguish three distinct milestones: request received, new admission stopped, and subsequent confirmation that running work has terminated.

### Admission boundaries and active generation {#sec-vol3-agent-harness-admission-boundaries}

A **turn boundary**\index{Turn boundary!definition} is an explicit checkpoint where the harness evaluates whether execution may proceed before admitting its next operation. Turn boundaries occur immediately before dispatching an inference call to a foundation model and immediately before invoking any external tool, including each individually admitted call within a proposed parallel batch. The name marks where control takes effect, not a boundary between turns: one turn (one step of the trajectory, counted by $\TurnHorizon$) contains a turn boundary before its model call and one before each tool call it admits. A pause that lands midway through a batch therefore leaves the calls already sent registered as owned work and withholds the rest. The admission check evaluates control flags under the trajectory record lock, and the release gate serializes its final decision with subsequent control updates. A flag check followed by an uncoordinated send would leave a race window and would not enforce this boundary. This boundary provides a local admission guarantee: instead of obscuring system state behind the timestamp of an operator's stop button, it leaves all remaining obligations explicit and inspectable.

Local candidate processing does not have to wait for remote model generation to finish. The foundation-model contract already separates a `CANCELED` reply from a `REJECTED` one and withholds both from dispatch; the harness turns that cancellation into a control action. It can initiate **streaming cancellation**\index{Streaming cancellation!definition}, commanding the serving engine to stop generating an in-progress reply, terminating the invocation's eligibility to produce an actionable candidate, and retaining partial output solely for bounded diagnosis. A canceled or truncated payload never becomes a dispatchable call, even if a tolerant JSON parser closes its dangling brackets, a valid tool-call prefix appeared before the abort signal, or an apparently complete response arrives after eligibility was withdrawn. The quarantining rule (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-status-envelope), an application of invariant closure (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}) to the reply status, holds regardless of how the invocation ended. Late-arriving evidence remains useful only to reconcile accounting usage or explain what the serving engine executed.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The distinction between rejected and canceled streamed replies, and the rule that a partial payload never reaches dispatch, are established in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-streaming-cancellation.
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-harness-boundary-wait
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TIME TO THE NEXT TURN BOUNDARY (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-controlplane-signals, "Output and time limits" paragraph.
# │ Goal: Show how long one admitted call can hold off the next turn boundary.
# │ Show: Reference per-token output allowance, a scenario output ceiling,
# │       and their product.
# │ How: Same registry path as the foundation-model cost cell: 8-bit weight
# │      bytes / accelerator bandwidth per generated token. No queueing,
# │      stalls, or serving overhead, so the product understates real waits.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import BYTES_INT8
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_count, fmt_time

class BoundaryWait:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    accel = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    weight_bytes = BYTES_INT8
    k_max = 4_096  # scenario: per-call output-token allowance

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    weights = model.parameters / ureg.param * weight_bytes
    t_dec = (weights / accel.memory.bandwidth).to(second)
    t_wait = (k_max * t_dec).to(second)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(60 * second < t_wait < 120 * second, "Boundary wait exceeds one minute")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_dec_ms_str = fmt_time(t_dec, unit=ms, precision=3)
    k_max_str = fmt_count(k_max)
    t_wait_str = fmt_time(t_wait, unit=second, precision=1)
```

Output allowances and wall-clock deadlines address fundamentally different operational risks. An output token ceiling enforces a hard boundary on generated volume under the serving engine's accounting contract; wall-clock latency, however, also depends on scheduling queues, network stalls, and autoregressive decode throughput. Even under ideal conditions, waiting for a full generation pass introduces substantial delay.[^fn-boundary-wait-batching] At a fixed per-token decode time, a call admitted with output allowance $\OutputLimit$, generating at $\PerTokenDecodeTime$, can postpone the next turn boundary by approximately

$$\TurnBoundaryDelay \approx \OutputLimit \times \PerTokenDecodeTime$$

Assuming an optimistic decode latency of `{python} BoundaryWait.t_dec_ms_str` per generated token, the single-accelerator, single-request floor of the estimate in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-per-call-work-estimate, with no queueing or memory-access stalls, a `{python} BoundaryWait.k_max_str`-token allowance postpones the boundary by roughly `{python} BoundaryWait.t_wait_str`. Pause or cancellation logic that passively waits for generation to complete would therefore block for more than a minute, and real serving queues only lengthen the wait. A node that splits the weights across several accelerators lowers the per-token floor but leaves the generation estimate linear in $\OutputLimit$, so halving the allowance halves the full-allowance generation time at a fixed rate, whereas streaming cancellation removes the dependence on generation length entirely. The harness uses both: turn boundaries govern discrete operation admission, while streaming cancellation stops active generations in flight.

[^fn-boundary-wait-batching]: **Why Batching Does Not Shorten the Wait**: The reference rate charges each generated token one full read of the weights, the single-request case. A serving engine that batches many requests shares that read among them, which raises throughput but still advances each request by one token per ordinary decode step, so batching cannot bring the per-request wait below this estimate. Techniques that emit several tokens per step change the rate, not the wait's linear growth with the output allowance. \index{Turn boundary!decode latency}

Stopping local execution is fundamentally different from terminating remote cluster execution. A host deadline determines when the supervisor ceases waiting and initiates intervention; confirming that remote inference has actually stopped requires positive evidence from the service. Under the settlement rule, unconfirmed resource usage remains an outstanding liability rather than an assumed refund.

### Pause and resume policy {#sec-vol3-agent-harness-pause-resume-policy}

The guarded pause sequence established in @sec-vol3-controlplane-statemachine holds new admissions while transitioning from `READY` to `PAUSED`. What this state means to an operator, however, depends on the policy configured for in-flight work. For the `r18` test, the policy may permit the active job to finish under its existing budget limits while holding the repair loop's continuation. Conversely, a policy requiring the job to stop immediately requests cancellation and records whatever outcome the executor confirms. A pause policy that permits execution to proceed leaves the workspace live and mutable, and the operator interface must reflect this active state. Any administrative inspection that demands quiescence requires positive confirmation that all concurrent writers have stopped, or else an isolated snapshot taken at a declared boundary. When the operator resumes the trajectory, execution proceeds along the guarded transitions defined in @sec-vol3-controlplane-statemachine; the pause policy governs only what ran while held, without altering the invariants enforced after resumption.

@Tbl-vol3-signal-vocabulary compares the requested changes to continuation.

| Request                         | Required control effect                                                            | Guarded outcome                                                              |
|:--------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Cancel                          | Hold new admission; request cancellation and account for owned work                | `FINALIZING`, then a recorded cancellation outcome when finalization permits |
| Interrupt with new instructions | Hold affected proposals; validate the instruction and revise its task dependencies | `READY` only when the revised continuation is eligible                       |
| Pause                           | Hold continuation and preserve an owner for outstanding work                       | `READY` to `PAUSED` with no runnable gap                                     |
| Resume                          | Reconcile evidence and recheck current permission and limits                       | `PAUSED` to `READY`, or remain held if guards fail                           |
| Kill                            | Stop admission and invoke available enforcement against active work                | `FINALIZING`, with confirmed and unresolved outcomes recorded                |
| Budget or deadline stop         | Deny further ordinary admission; preserve funded finalization duties               | `FINALIZING`, with the stopping reason and remaining obligations             |

: **Control requests and their enforced scope**: A control action changes admission and continuation through the guarded lifecycle. Cancellation and termination of already admitted work require separate evidence. {#tbl-vol3-signal-vocabulary tbl-colwidths="[22,41,37]"}

Mid-trajectory user steering demands the same transactional discipline. If an operator injects a steering instruction, such as directing the agent to modify a different target file, the harness cannot simply append the prompt to the conversation context and assume existing operations adapt. Adding instructions does not retroactively invalidate an already admitted file edit or revoke an active tool approval. Instead, the harness records the instruction, determines which plan steps and proposed actions are superseded, and verifies whether outstanding operations conflict with the revised task.

### Termination and remaining obligations {#sec-vol3-agent-harness-termination-obligations}

Unlike cooperative cancellation, a kill request invokes immediate, non-cooperative enforcement. Trajectory-level encapsulation (principle \ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation})\index{Principle!trajectory-level encapsulation} is what makes this enforcement possible: because control requests are recorded independently of model output, the runtime can stop new admission and abort the local work it supervises without waiting on the model or on an external service's response. When a kill signal arrives, the controller halts local execution, revokes mediated access tokens, and fences off obsolete workers across the execution paths under its control. The sandbox reset contract in @sec-vol3-sandboxes-pooling-reset determines which child processes, descendant namespaces, network channels, and allocated resources that enforcement covers. Asynchronous remote work, third-party transactions, and external handles lie beyond direct local process control and demand their own corroborating evidence.

Finalization therefore records confirmed termination separately from unresolved side effects and pending charges, which retain their designated owner under the settlement rule. The operation's repeat contract determines whether another attempt is safe, and settlement must precede any retry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement}); an operation identifier alone cannot reveal what the interrupted execution actually modified.

Enforcing external control decouples trajectory continuation from model behavior and frees execution resources. Worker threads and compute slots never remain blocked while an external job or cancellation response is outstanding. By persisting these control directives and outstanding obligations within the trajectory record, the harness safely suspends execution and yields worker resources, admitting continuation only when verified events satisfy the state machine's guards.

## Supervised Waiting {#sec-vol3-controlplane-yielding}

When the agent dispatches the integration test for candidate `r18`, the model generates nothing for as long as the test runs, which is tens of seconds for the integration test priced in notebook \ref{nbk-05-residency-tax}, and minutes for a broader suite. If the worker thread that dispatched the job blocks until the result returns, it cannot service any other trajectory in the interim. Worse, the runtime becomes unresponsive to operator pauses or high-priority interactive requests. The repair trajectory requires no token generation while the test executes. What it requires instead is an external supervisor: a control entity that tracks the in-flight job, holds the execution continuation, and buffers incoming evidence without tying up a worker thread in a synchronous wait.

Yielding execution through an asynchronous wait[^fn-worker-release-seda] releases the worker thread immediately, leaving the trajectory record as the explicit holder of pending state. Alternatively, a runtime with blocking workers can maintain controllability if an independent supervisor thread handles operator requests, heartbeats, and deadlines. This architectural requirement transcends any specific event-loop implementation: waiting must keep the control record accessible, and any returning event must pass through that record's admission guards before advancing the trajectory.

[^fn-worker-release-seda]: **Event-Driven Waiting**: Internet servers faced the thread-per-request version of this problem when a request could wait far longer than it computed. SEDA [@welsh2001seda] split services into event-driven stages joined by explicit queues and applied admission control at each queue, so load was visible and bounded where work waited rather than hidden in blocked threads. A harness whose tool jobs run for minutes while a model call takes seconds has the same shape, and the trajectory record is its queue entry. \index{Staged event-driven architecture!agent waiting}

### The result wakeup pipeline {#sec-vol3-agent-harness-wakeup-pipeline}

The asynchronous job interface decouples job acceptance from completion, so a result can arrive seconds or hours after dispatch, out of order, or more than once. The register-before-send rule makes that safe. For an external job, registration records the owning trajectory, the invocation and attempt identifiers, the external job handle when available, the expected workspace source revision, the observation eligibility policy, and the outstanding liability, so even an immediate callback finds the record it needs.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The asynchronous tool invocation interface and completion polling contracts are established in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-async.
:::

Regardless of how the runtime structures concurrency, the supervisor must satisfy four distinct logical obligations when processing an incoming result. @Tbl-vol3-event-wakeup-pipeline stages them in order and pairs each with the inference it does not license.
